title: Performance Optimization
description: Optimize EF Core performance using AsNoTracking, compiled queries, batch operations, and strategies to avoid common performance pitfalls like N+1 queries.

blocks.text: Why EF Core Performance Matters

EF Core is powerful, but it can be slow if used carelessly. The most common performance problems are N+1 queries (fetching related data one row at a time), tracking entities unnecessarily, and loading entire tables when only a few columns are needed. Understanding how EF Core works internally helps you avoid these traps.

This lesson covers the most important EF Core performance techniques: disabling change tracking for read-only queries, using compiled queries to reduce translation overhead, batching multiple operations, and detecting common pitfalls before they reach production.
Change Tracking Overhead

Every entity loaded by EF Core is tracked by default. The change tracker maintains a snapshot of the original property values so it can detect what changed when you call SaveChangesAsync. For read-only queries where you never modify the entities, this tracking work is wasted.

AsNoTracking tells EF Core to skip change tracking for a query. This is significantly faster for read-only scenarios and reduces memory usage because EF Core does not need to maintain the original value snapshots.

blocks.title: AsNoTracking for read-only queries
blocks.content: Fetching products for display in a read-only list without change tracking overhead.

blocks.title: Tip: Use AsNoTracking for read-only scenarios
blocks.text: Any query that only reads data for display — like product listings, search results, or report data — should use AsNoTracking. It can improve query performance by 20-50% for large result sets.
Avoiding the N+1 Query Problem

The N+1 query problem is the most common EF Core performance anti-pattern. It happens when you load a list of entities and then access a navigation property for each one in a loop. EF Core issues one query for the list and then N additional queries for the related data.

blocks.title: N+1 problem and its fix
blocks.content: Comparing lazy loading (N+1 queries) with eager loading (single query).

blocks.text: In the N+1 example, accessing product.Category.Name inside the loop causes EF Core to issue a separate SELECT query for each product's category. For 50 products, that is 51 database round trips instead of one. The fix is to use Include to load the related data in the initial query.

blocks.title: Warning: Always profile your queries
blocks.text: The N+1 problem is invisible in code and only shows up when you look at the executed SQL. Enable logging to see the queries your application is generating, or use tools like MiniProfiler to detect excessive database calls.
Compiled Queries

Every time you execute a LINQ query, EF Core translates it into SQL. This translation has a small but measurable cost, especially for frequently executed queries. Compiled queries cache the translation result, skipping the LINQ-to-SQL conversion on subsequent executions.

In EF Core 7+, you can use compiled queries with the new CompiledQuery type. In earlier versions, you use EF.CompileQuery. Compiled queries are most beneficial for hot paths that execute thousands of times per second.

blocks.title: Compiled query for frequently executed lookups
blocks.content: Creating and using a compiled query to fetch a product by name.

blocks.text: The compiled query is defined as a static readonly field. EF Core builds the SQL once when the application starts and reuses it for every call. The only thing that changes per call is the parameter value, which is passed efficiently to the database.
Batching Operations

When inserting, updating, or deleting multiple entities, use batch operations to reduce round trips to the database. EF Core 7+ supports ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete, which translate to single SQL UPDATE or DELETE statements without loading entities into memory.

blocks.title: Batch update and delete without loading entities
blocks.content: Using ExecuteUpdateAsync and ExecuteDeleteAsync for efficient bulk operations.

blocks.text: Before EF Core 7, you would have to load all matching entities into memory, modify them, and call SaveChangesAsync. This was slow and memory-intensive. ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete push the operation to the database, processing all matching rows in a single round trip.
Other Performance Tips

Beyond the techniques above, several other practices help keep EF Core fast in production. Avoid loading entire tables when you only need a subset, use projection to fetch only required columns, and be cautious with lazy loading in hot paths.

blocks.title: Additional performance best practices
items: Use projection with Select to fetch only the columns you need rather than loading full entities
Avoid loading entire tables — always use Where or pagination
Use split queries when Include loads too many related entities, reducing JOIN complexity
Cache frequently accessed reference data like product categories in memory
Monitor generated SQL using logging to identify slow or unexpected queries

blocks.title: Tip: Enable SQL logging during development
blocks.text: Call logging.AddConsole() in Program.cs or set the log level to Information for Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command to see every SQL query. This is invaluable for spotting N+1 problems and verifying that indexes are being used.

blocks.title: Identify and Fix Performance Issues
blocks.description: Profile an existing EF Core codebase, identify N+1 queries, and apply optimizations including AsNoTracking and projection.
steps: Create a new project with EF Core, SQLite, and at least two entities with a one-to-many relationship
Seed the database with 100 products across 5 categories
Write a method that loads all products and accesses each product's Category.Name in a loop — observe the N+1 problem
Enable EF Core SQL logging to console to verify multiple queries are being issued
Fix the N+1 problem by adding Include and measure the reduction in queries
Rewrite the query using AsNoTracking and projection to a DTO, measuring the performance difference
Add a compiled query for the most frequently executed lookup and verify it works correctly
blocks.expectedOutcome: The N+1 version issues over 100 queries for 100 products. The Include version issues 1 query. The projected AsNoTracking version issues 1 query with less data transferred. The compiled query produces identical results with reduced translation overhead.

blocks.title: Performance Optimization Summary
points: Change tracking has overhead — use AsNoTracking for read-only queries
The N+1 problem occurs when navigation properties are accessed in loops without Include
Eager loading with Include prevents N+1 queries by fetching related data in one round trip
Compiled queries cache LINQ-to-SQL translations for frequently executed hot paths
ExecuteUpdate and ExecuteDelete perform bulk operations in SQL without loading entities
Always profile generated SQL to catch performance problems before they reach production
blocks.takeaway: EF Core performance is not automatic — it requires intentional choices about tracking, loading strategy, and query shape. The difference between a slow and fast EF Core application often comes down to using AsNoTracking, Include, and compiled queries consistently.
